items.passage:
The Boy Who Cried Wolf

A shepherd boy looked after the sheep on a hill above the village. It was a long, quiet job, and the boy was bored.

One day he had an idea. He ran down the hill shouting, “Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is chasing the sheep!”

The villagers dropped their tools and raced up the hill to help. But there was no wolf. The boy laughed and laughed.

A week later, he did it again. “Wolf! Wolf!” Again the villagers ran up the hill, puffing and panting. Again there was no wolf. They were cross.

Then one evening, a real wolf crept out of the forest. The boy screamed, “Wolf! Wolf! Please help!”

But this time nobody came. “He is just playing his tricks again,” they said.

Nobody believes a liar, even when he is telling the truth.

items.passage:
The Ant and the Grasshopper

All summer long, the grasshopper sang and danced in the warm sunshine.

The ant was busy. Up and down the path she went, carrying grains of corn to her nest, one at a time.

“Why are you working so hard?” asked the grasshopper. “Come and play!”

“I am storing food for the winter,” said the ant. “You should do the same.”

The grasshopper laughed. “Winter is ages away! There is plenty of food now.”

But winter came. Snow covered the fields, and there was no food to be found. The hungry grasshopper knocked on the ant’s door.

The ant had plenty to eat. She shared a little with the grasshopper, and said, “Next summer, remember: work today, and you will be ready for tomorrow.”

items.passage:
The North Wind and the Sun

The North Wind and the Sun were arguing about who was the strongest.

“Let’s have a contest,” said the Sun. “Do you see that traveller walking down the road? Whoever can make him take off his coat is the strongest.”

The North Wind went first. He blew and he blew. He blew so hard that leaves flew off the trees. But the harder he blew, the tighter the traveller wrapped his coat around himself.

At last the North Wind gave up.

Then it was the Sun’s turn. The Sun came out from behind a cloud and shone gently down. The traveller grew warmer and warmer. Soon he unbuttoned his coat. Then he took it off altogether and sat down in the shade.

Kindness can win where force fails.

items.passage:
The Fox and the Grapes

One hot day, a hungry fox was walking through an orchard. High above him, on a vine, hung a bunch of juicy purple grapes.

“Just what I need,” said the fox, licking his lips.

He took a run and jumped, but he missed. He tried again, jumping higher, but the grapes were still out of reach. Again and again he jumped, until he was hot and tired.

At last he gave up and walked away with his nose in the air.

“I didn’t want them anyway,” he said. “I am sure they are sour.”

It is easy to pretend you don’t want something when you can’t have it.

The Fox and the Grapes

One hot day, a hungry fox was walking through an orchard. High above him, on a vine, hung a bunch of juicy purple grapes.

“Just what I need,” said the fox, licking his lips.

He took a run and jumped, but he missed. He tried again, jumping higher, but the grapes were still out of reach. Again and again he jumped, until he was hot and tired.

At last he gave up and walked away with his nose in the air.

“I didn’t want them anyway,” he said. “I am sure they are sour.”

It is easy to pretend you don’t want something when you can’t have it.

Two Seconds

Rosa was the newest member of the pit crew. Her job was the front left tyre.

All week she had practised. Wheel gun on, nut off, old tyre out, new tyre in, nut on. Again and again, until her arms ached. On Friday she was still too slow. “Don’t worry,” said Sam, the crew chief. “Keep practising.”

On race day, the cars thundered round the track. The noise was so loud that Rosa could feel it in her chest.

Then the radio crackled: “Box, box, box!” Their car was coming in.

Rosa’s heart pounded. The car screeched into the pit lane and stopped exactly on the line. Rosa did not think. Her hands remembered everything. Nut off, tyre out, tyre in, nut on. She raised her hand. Done!

The car roared away. Sam looked at the clock and grinned. “Two seconds,” he said. “The fastest stop of the day.”

The Rover Who Kept Going

Far away, on the dusty red planet Mars, a little rover called Dot rolled slowly across the rocks.

Dot had six wheels, a camera on a long neck and a robot arm for picking up stones. Every day, scientists on Earth sent Dot a list of jobs. Every day, Dot did them, then sent back photographs.

One morning a dust storm swept across the planet. The sky turned dark orange. Dust covered Dot’s solar panels, and without sunlight her batteries began to run low.

Dot went to sleep to save power. On Earth, the scientists waited. Days passed. Weeks passed. Some people said, “We have lost her.”

Then one day the wind changed. It blew the dust off Dot’s panels. The Sun shone on them again, and Dot’s batteries slowly filled up.

Beep. A message arrived on Earth. The scientists cheered and hugged each other. Dot was awake, and ready for work.

The driver climbed down, shaking. “Thank you,” he said. “You saved us all.”

items.passage:
Fact file: Emperor penguins

Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins in the world. They can grow to more than a metre tall, about as tall as a six-year-old child.

They live in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth. To keep warm, they have a thick layer of fat called blubber, and tightly packed feathers.

Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Instead, they are amazing swimmers. They use their flippers like wings to “fly” through the water, catching fish and squid.

At the start of winter, the mother penguin lays one egg. Then she goes to sea to feed. The father keeps the egg warm on his feet, under a flap of skin, for about two months. He eats nothing at all until she comes back!

items.passage:
Fact file: Volcanoes

Deep under the ground, it is so hot that rock melts. This melted rock is called magma.

A volcano is an opening in the Earth’s surface. When a volcano erupts, magma bursts out. Once it comes out of the ground, we call it lava. Lava can be as hot as 1,000 degrees Celsius, ten times hotter than boiling water!

Volcanoes can also throw out clouds of ash and gas. Long ago, in the year 79, a volcano in Italy called Vesuvius erupted. Its ash buried the Roman town of Pompeii. Today we can walk through its streets and see how the Romans lived.

Scientists who study volcanoes are called volcanologists. They watch for clues, like small earthquakes, that a volcano might be about to erupt.

items.passage:
Fact file: Dinosaurs

Dinosaurs lived on Earth for millions of years. The last dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, long before there were any people.

The word “dinosaur” means “terrible lizard”. Some dinosaurs were as small as a chicken. Others were as long as three buses!

Some dinosaurs, like Tyrannosaurus rex, were carnivores: they ate meat. T. rex had teeth as long as bananas. Others, like Stegosaurus and Triceratops, were herbivores: they ate plants.

The Spitfire was a fighter plane with room for just one pilot. It had a powerful engine called the Merlin, and special curved wings shaped like an oval. These wings helped it to turn very quickly.

In the summer of 1940, during the Second World War, Spitfires and Hurricanes flew in the Battle of Britain. Their pilots stopped enemy planes from taking control of the skies over Britain.

People all over Britain gave money to help build more Spitfires. Some even gave their old pots and pans so the metal could be used!

Today, a few Spitfires still fly at air shows. The sound of their engines is unforgettable.

Fact file: How to become a knight

In the Middle Ages, a boy who wanted to be a knight had to train for many years.

At about seven years old, he went to live in a lord’s castle as a page. He learned good manners, and how to ride a horse.

At about fourteen, he became a squire. A squire looked after a knight’s armour and horse, and practised fighting with a sword and lance.

At about twenty-one, if he had trained well, the squire was made a knight. He knelt in front of the lord or the king, who tapped him on the shoulder with a sword. This was called being dubbed.

Knights wore armour made of metal. Each knight had a coat of arms on his shield, so that people could tell who he was when his face was hidden by his helmet.

items.passage:
This is a Tale about a tail—a tail that belonged to a little red squirrel, and his name was Nutkin.

He had a brother called Twinkleberry, and a great many cousins: they lived in a wood at the edge of a lake.

In the middle of the lake there is an island covered with trees and nut bushes; and amongst those trees stands a hollow oak-tree, which is the house of an owl who is called Old Brown.

One autumn when the nuts were ripe, and the leaves on the hazel bushes were golden and green—Nutkin and Twinkleberry and all the other little squirrels came out of the wood, and down to the edge of the lake.

They made little rafts out of twigs, and they paddled away over the water to Owl Island to gather nuts.

Each squirrel had a little sack and a large oar, and spread out his tail for a sail.

They also took with them an offering of three fat mice as a present for Old Brown, and put them down upon his door-step.

Then Twinkleberry and the other little squirrels each made a low bow, and said politely—

“Old Mr. Brown, will you favour us with permission to gather nuts upon your island?”

But Nutkin was excessively impertinent in his manners. He bobbed up and down like a little red cherry, singing—

“Riddle me, riddle me, rot-tot-tote!
A little wee man, in a red red coat!
A staff in his hand, and a stone in his throat;
If you’ll tell me this riddle, I’ll give you a groat.”

Now this riddle is as old as the hills; Mr. Brown paid no attention whatever to Nutkin.

He shut his eyes obstinately and went to sleep.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Squirrel Nutkin (1903)

“Riddle me, riddle me, rot-tot-tote!
A little wee man, in a red red coat!
A staff in his hand, and a stone in his throat;
If you’ll tell me this riddle, I’ll give you a groat.”

Now this riddle is as old as the hills; Mr. Brown paid no attention whatever to Nutkin.

Dark brown is the river,
Golden is the sand.

Away down the hill.

items.explain: “There were thousands of millions of stars.”
items.passage:
The lights from the parlour and kitchen shone out
Through the blinds and the windows and bars;
And high overhead and all moving about,
There were thousands of millions of stars.
There ne’er were such thousands of leaves on a tree,
Nor of people in church or the Park,
As the crowds of the stars that looked down upon me,
And that glittered and winked in the dark.

The Dog, and the Plough, and the Hunter, and all,
And the star of the sailor, and Mars,
These shone in the sky, and the pail by the wall
Would be half full of water and stars.
They saw me at last, and they chased me with cries,
And they soon had me packed into bed;
But the glory kept shining and bright in my eyes,
And the stars going round in my head.
items.passageSource: Robert Louis Stevenson, “Escape at Bedtime”, A Child’s Garden of Verses (1885)
